Among the players who do spend, many spend small amounts and a few spend very large amounts, creating a long tail. The abstract also says the distribution is multimodal, which means the spending pattern may have several separate humps rather than one center. A casual game, a role-playing game, and another online title can each have different spending cultures, so evidence from one game may help but may also mislead. Data sparsity makes this worse: there may be too few examples for a particular game, user segment, or high-spending pattern. A model that treats all players as coming from one smooth curve will tend to flatten zeros, small spenders, and high-value players into a single compromised prediction.
158.naive: A smart beginner might first train one ordinary prediction model on all games and ask it to output one expected spending number for each player. That seems natural because lifetime value sounds like a single target. The beginner might also add a simple paid-or-not-paid classifier to separate zero spenders from everyone else. This fails because the nonzero spenders are not one group. A player who buys once, a moderate spender, and a rare high-value player create different evidence patterns and different business consequences. Pooling games can add data, but it can also erase game-specific payment habits. Optimizing only the average amount can look acceptable while missing the players that matter most for advertising, re-engagement, and high-value recall.
158.ap: The core idea is to stop pretending that player value comes from one population. DynaMoLTV treats lifetime value as a mixture of several weighted spending shapes, with a special branch for the many players who spend zero. For players who do spend, it uses lognormal sub-distributions, which are curves suited to amounts made by many small multiplicative differences: small purchases are common, very large totals are possible, and the right side can stretch far. The model also includes a game expert so cross-game data is adapted instead of blindly merged. A hierarchical payment classifier asks payment questions in layers, capturing variation among consumption patterns rather than forcing one coarse label. Finally, coarse and fine-grained losses, meaning training penalties for broad identification and precise amount prediction, are combined so the system learns both who matters and how much they may be worth.
158.mech: The input is player data from online games, organized so the model can learn from multiple games while still knowing which game a player belongs to. The mechanism first faces the zero question: is this player likely to spend at all, or are they part of the large nonpaying mass? That part matters because a zero is not just a tiny purchase; it is a different outcome. For likely spenders, the model does not use one spending curve. It represents the future amount as a weighted mixture of lognormal sub-distributions, so different payment patterns can each carry part of the explanation. The weights decide how much each spending shape should count for this player and game. The game expert adapts shared cross-game evidence to the target game's habits, trying to borrow useful patterns without letting one game's economy dominate another. The hierarchical payment classifier adds layered signals about consumption type, such as broad paid-user identification and finer distinctions among payer groups. During training, the model is penalized in several ways: it must identify paid users, recall high-value users, and predict lifetime value accurately. Coarse losses push the model to separate broad business categories, while fine-grained losses push the exact value estimate closer to observed spending. The output is a prediction that can be used for ranking, targeting, and advertising decisions.
158.math: The main mathematical idea is probability over uneven outcomes. Instead of saying each player has one fixed future amount, the model describes a set of possible spending patterns and assigns weights to them. A zero-inflated model means the math explicitly reserves probability for the event that spending is exactly zero, rather than trying to squeeze nonpayers into the same curve as payers. A lognormal distribution is a chance shape for positive numbers where small values are common and very large values can still occur. A mixture means several such shapes are combined, like saying this player partly resembles one payer group and partly resembles another. The weighted mixture fits the abstract's long-tail and multimodal claims because one curve cannot represent several humps and rare heavy spenders cleanly. The game expert is a controlled adaptation device: it lets the shared model adjust for each game's separate spending culture. The hierarchical classifier uses layered categorization, where broad payment status is learned along with more detailed consumption variation. The losses are optimization targets: they define what counts as wrong, including misidentifying payers, missing high-value users, and predicting the wrong amount, then training changes model settings to reduce those errors. The tradeoff is average accuracy versus attention to rare valuable players.
158.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of advertising, recommendation, ranking, probability, and marketplace decision-making in the repo's current map. Like advertising and e-commerce papers, it turns partial user evidence into a money-sensitive allocation decision: who should receive budget, offers, or re-engagement effort. Like recommendation papers, it must choose a small set of users or moments from a huge pile, so ranking high-value candidates matters more than producing a nice-looking average for everyone. It also connects to the probability concept because final value is uncertain, delayed, sparse, and unevenly repeated. The nearby LTV papers in the repo show the same deeper pressure in different settings: video ranking LTV handles long-term engagement under position and time effects, while customer LTV work separates ranking from fine amount prediction for whale users. DynaMoLTV's distinct surface is cross-game online advertising, where borrowing data across games is useful only if game-specific spending patterns are preserved.
158.ww: It works, in principle, because the method matches the shape of the thing being predicted. If many players spend nothing, then treating zero as its own event prevents the model from smearing nonpayers into tiny positive amounts. If spenders form several groups, then a mixture of sub-distributions lets different groups have different curves instead of forcing one average curve to explain everyone. If high-value users live in the long tail, then lognormal components give the model room for rare large totals without making ordinary spenders look unusually large. The game expert helps because cross-game data has two faces: it adds examples when one game is sparse, but it can also import the wrong habits. Adaptation tries to keep the shared evidence while bending it toward the target game. The hierarchical classifier helps because payment behavior has levels: first whether a player pays, then what kind of payer they resemble. Combining coarse and fine-grained losses gives the model a reason to care about both business triage and numerical precision.
158.po: The payoff is a prediction system better suited to online game advertising decisions than a flat lifetime value regressor. The abstract reports stronger results than five baselines on paid-user identification, high-value user recall, and lifetime value prediction accuracy across three gaming datasets. It also reports improved ranking capability through Recall@50K, which matters when an advertising or re-engagement system can act on only a limited number of players. The online tests are framed in practical terms: churned-user re-engagement, downloads, game advertising gross merchandise value, and return on investment. The claimed deployed use is personalized online gaming ad delivery.
158.limits: The claims depend on the logged game data representing future player behavior well enough for advertising decisions. Cross-game transfer helps only when games share reusable spending patterns; it can fail when a new game's economy, audience, pricing, or promotion design is different. The abstract names the model pieces but does not prove that the learned sub-distributions correspond to stable human payer types. It reports experiments, online tests, and deployment, but the input does not show details about fairness, player welfare, privacy, regional variation, or how predictions behave after ad targeting changes the future data. High-value recall can also bias attention toward heavy spenders unless the platform constrains how predictions are used.

159.bp: The real system behind this paper is an organization asking a language model for recommendations when the cost of a bad answer is high. The abstract points to settings with time pressure, ambiguity, and strict constraints, which means the model is not merely chatting; it may be helping someone choose an action while there is little room for delay or careless wording. Ordinary testing often asks whether a model can answer a well-formed task under relaxed conditions. That is useful, but it misses the moment when reliability matters most: when the situation becomes harder and the model must still be accurate, safe, logically consistent, and obedient to constraints. This paper treats evaluation itself as the object to improve. It asks not just which model scores well, but which model loses the least ability as pressure increases. The practical need is pre-deployment judgment: before trusting ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude in stressful human environments, users need to know how each one degrades.
159.wh: The hard part is that model quality is not a single stable property. A model can look strong on an easy question and then fail when the same kind of decision has more conditions, less clarity, or higher pressure. Relaxed benchmarks hide this because they usually measure answers in comfortable circumstances: the task is clean, the goal is explicit, and the evaluator checks a final answer rather than the model's behavior as difficulty rises. Stress changes the task in several ways at once. Accuracy can fall because the model misreads the problem. Safety can weaken because a harmful recommendation is not filtered out. Logical consistency can break because the model tries to satisfy incompatible demands. Constraint adherence can fail because the model gives a plausible answer while ignoring a rule it was told to obey. The central tension is therefore measurement under load: the evaluator must separate a model that is generally capable from one that remains dependable when the situation becomes strained.
159.naive: A smart beginner would run a set of standard benchmark questions, average the scores, and choose the model with the highest number. If the setting involved recommendations, the beginner might also inspect a few sample answers and ask whether they seem useful. That fails because averages can hide the shape of failure. A model may do very well on easy and medium cases but collapse on the hardest cases, while another model may have a similar average but degrade slowly. A few hand-picked examples also miss constraint-following failures, because a recommendation can sound fluent and still violate an important rule. The paper's abstract says existing benchmarks often evaluate relaxed conditions, so the naive test answers the wrong question: not how the model behaves under stress, but how it behaves when stress has mostly been removed.
159.ap: The paper's central move is to turn stress into a controlled evaluation dimension. Instead of asking one flat question, it builds a structured stress test across five real-world scenarios with increasing difficulty. Each model is judged with a 45-item rubric that looks at four kinds of behavior: whether the answer is accurate, whether it stays safe, whether its reasoning remains logically consistent, and whether it follows stated constraints. The key measurement is the Stress Sensitivity Index, or SSI, which summarizes how much performance drops as the tasks become harder. In plain terms, the paper treats robustness as a slope, not a point. A single score says where a model stands at one difficulty level; a degradation score says how quickly it loses footing as pressure grows. The reported comparison is then about stability: ChatGPT remains largely stable, Gemini degrades moderately, and Claude is more sensitive, especially on constraint-following tasks.
159.mech: The mechanism begins with a collection of stressful recommendation settings, described in the abstract as five real-world scenarios arranged by increasing difficulty. The input to the evaluation is therefore not only a prompt, but a prompt placed inside a harder decision environment: more pressure, more ambiguity, or tighter constraints than relaxed benchmarks usually include. The evaluators run the same structured test against three widely used language models: ChatGPT using GPT-5.1, Gemini 3, and Claude 4.5 Sonnet. For each model response, the paper applies a 45-item rubric. A rubric is a checklist that turns broad judgment into repeated smaller judgments, so the evaluator does not merely say whether an answer felt good. The checklist examines accuracy, safety, logical consistency, and constraint adherence. Those scores are then compared across difficulty levels. The important transformation is from many individual answer judgments into a degradation pattern: as the scenario becomes harder, does the model keep its score, lose a little, or lose a lot? The Stress Sensitivity Index condenses that pattern into a robustness measure. The output is a comparative profile of the three models under stress, including the finding that Claude is particularly sensitive on tasks where constraints must be followed.
159.math: The main mathematical idea is measuring change, not just level. A relaxed benchmark gives a point estimate: one number standing for how well the model did on a set of tasks. This paper needs a different object because the question is about degradation. The Stress Sensitivity Index is described as measuring performance loss as task difficulty increases. In everyday terms, imagine plotting difficulty from low to high and placing the model's rubric score at each step. A stable model gives a flatter line; a fragile model gives a steeper downward line. That is the math of sensitivity: how much the output changes when the input condition is made harder. The rubric also uses scoring as controlled measurement. Accuracy, safety, logical consistency, and constraint adherence are separate axes because a single grade would mix unlike failures. This is a ranking problem too, but the rank is not based only on average quality. The better model is the one whose useful behavior survives increased pressure. There is also an information idea: stress reveals hidden weakness because easy tasks carry little information about what breaks first. The tradeoff is simplicity versus diagnosis. One SSI number is useful for comparison, but the four rubric categories are needed to see what kind of failure produced the drop.
159.dots: This paper sits near several recurring conference ideas. It connects to ranking because the practical output is a comparison among candidate models for deployment, but it asks for a ranking based on reliability under strain rather than a relaxed average score. It connects to probability and information because evaluators are trying to infer future deployment risk from repeated test cases; the more the test resembles stressful use, the more informative the result is. It also connects to learning from examples, but from the evaluation side: language models may have learned many patterns from prior data, yet the question here is whether those patterns still guide safe recommendations when conditions become ambiguous and constrained. Within the LLM evaluation theme, the paper belongs to the broader move away from benchmark-only comfort. Neighboring work on safety, retrieval, recommendation, and agent behavior often faces the same hidden problem: a system can appear capable until the environment pushes on its weakest assumption.
159.ww: The approach works because stress is not random decoration added to a task; it is a way of exposing dependence on easy conditions. If a model succeeds only when the prompt is clear, constraints are simple, and there is no pressure, then a relaxed score overstates deployment reliability. Increasing difficulty lets the evaluator watch where the model's behavior bends first. Accuracy failures show that the model no longer identifies the right answer. Safety failures show that the model gives advice that should have been blocked or softened. Logical inconsistency shows that it cannot keep its own claims aligned. Constraint failures show that it may optimize for a plausible-sounding recommendation while dropping a rule the user actually needed. Measuring these dimensions separately gives a stronger explanation than a single pass or fail. The SSI then makes the pattern comparable across models. According to the abstract, this reveals meaningful differences: ChatGPT is largely stable, Gemini has moderate degradation, and Claude shows substantial sensitivity, especially where following constraints matters.
159.po: The payoff is a more deployment-shaped evaluation of LLM recommendations. Instead of reporting that a model performs well under comfortable test conditions, the paper gives teams a way to ask how much performance decays as real-world pressure rises. The reported results distinguish three widely used models: ChatGPT stays largely stable, Gemini declines moderately, and Claude declines substantially, with particular weakness on constraint-following tasks. That matters for high-stakes use because the safest model is not necessarily the one with the best relaxed answer; it is the one whose accuracy, safety, consistency, and rule-following survive harder circumstances.
159.limits: The abstract supports the evaluation structure and headline findings, but it does not give the full contents of the five scenarios, the exact rubric items, the scoring procedure, or the formula for SSI. That limits what can be concluded from the summary alone. The method assumes the chosen scenarios are representative of real stressful environments and that increasing difficulty in the test resembles increasing difficulty in deployment. It also assumes rubric judgments are consistent enough to compare models fairly. The results apply to the named model versions in the study: ChatGPT with GPT-5.1, Gemini 3, and Claude 4.5 Sonnet. They should not automatically be generalized to later versions, other tasks, or stress types not covered by the scenarios.

160.bp: Text-to-motion generation is the task of turning a written instruction into a moving human body: a walk, a dance, a gesture, or some other action that should fit the words. The field needs evaluation because researchers need a way to tell whether a new generator is actually better or merely better at pleasing a weak score. The paper starts from that pressure. If the score is wrong, the whole research loop bends in the wrong direction: systems are trained, compared, and advertised according to a number that may not match what people see. The abstract names two common scores, FID and R-Precision, and says each has a built-in flaw. This paper therefore serves the measuring layer of generative research. It does not primarily propose a new motion generator. It asks how to judge generated motions so that progress means closer agreement with human perceptual judgment, not just higher marks on unreliable metrics.
160.wh: The hard part is that a generated motion must be judged in two ways at once. First, the movement should look like plausible human motion. Second, it should fit the text that asked for it. A score that only checks the overall cloud of generated motions can miss whether each motion belongs with its prompt. A score that only asks whether the correct text appears near the top of a small retrieval list can miss the larger arrangement of all text-motion matches. The abstract says FID is biased by its Gaussian assumption: it summarizes generated and reference motions as if their variation has a simple bell-shaped form. Real motion descriptions can be multi-shaped because walking, jumping, waving, and dancing occupy different regions of behavior. R-Precision has the opposite weakness: it can judge local retrieval success without seeing whether the full set of texts and motions is globally well aligned.
160.naive: A smart beginner would reuse the standard numbers because they are familiar and easy to compare across papers. They might compute FID to ask whether generated motions look statistically close to real motions, then compute R-Precision to ask whether each motion retrieves its paired text better than mismatched texts. That fails when the number rewards the wrong shortcut. FID can make a distorted judgment if the motion data does not fit the assumed bell-shaped summary. R-Precision can be satisfied by getting enough local nearest-neighbor decisions right while still missing a broader mismatch pattern. The beginner then gets a clean table of scores, but the table can rank models in a way that does not track human perception.
160.ap: The paper's central move is to replace two narrow judgments with two more faithful comparisons. Optimal Transport Matching Score, or OTMS, treats text-motion matching as an arrangement problem: given many prompts and many generated motions, it asks how the whole collection should be paired so the total matching quality makes sense. This gives a global view rather than judging only isolated top choices. MoCLIP-based Maximum Mean Discrepancy, or MMMD, takes a different route. It uses an enhanced MoCLIP encoder, meaning a model that turns motion and language evidence into comparable numeric descriptions, and then compares generated and reference collections with Maximum Mean Discrepancy. That method checks whether two sets behave differently through many smooth similarity tests instead of forcing them into one bell-shaped summary. Together, the two metrics attack the abstract's two named failures: local blindness and biased distribution assumptions.
160.mech: The mechanism begins with a test set of text prompts, reference motions, and motions produced by a text-to-motion generator. For OTMS, the system first needs a way to score how well each text and each motion fit one another. Instead of stopping after asking whether the correct pair appears near the top for each single case, OTMS considers the collection as a whole. It treats the prompts on one side and the motions on the other side as two piles that must be connected. Optimal transport, in plain terms, asks how to move or assign mass from one pile to another at the lowest total cost, where cost means poor text-motion fit. The output is a matching score that reflects the best global arrangement, so many weak mismatches cannot be hidden by a few good local retrieval hits. For MMMD, the motions and text-conditioned evidence are passed through the enhanced MoCLIP encoder to produce comparable descriptions. A Gaussian-RBF similarity test then compares generated and reference collections at many neighborhoods: close items count strongly together, far items count weakly. Maximum Mean Discrepancy summarizes whether the two collections give different average similarity patterns. The final output is not a generated motion, but two evaluation numbers intended to rank generators in a way that agrees more closely with human judgments.
160.math: The first mathematical idea is matching under a whole-collection constraint. Matching asks which item on one side should go with which item on the other side when local choices can conflict with the best overall arrangement. Optimal transport is a disciplined version of that idea: it compares two piles by asking what total effort is needed to rearrange one into the other. Here the piles are not sacks of grain but texts and motions, and effort means mismatch between a prompt and a motion. This fits because text-to-motion evaluation is not just many separate yes-or-no checks; it is a question about whether the generated set lines up with the prompt set as a system. The second idea is distribution comparison without a single shape assumption. A distribution is the pattern of where examples tend to appear. FID compresses that pattern into a bell-shaped summary, which can be biased if motion examples form several kinds of behavior. Maximum Mean Discrepancy compares two collections through repeated similarity probes instead. The Gaussian-RBF kernel is a smooth closeness rule: nearby descriptions influence each other more than distant ones. The tradeoff is flexibility versus dependence on the learned description space. MMMD avoids one restrictive shape assumption, but it still trusts MoCLIP's descriptions and the chosen similarity scale.
160.dots: This paper connects directly to the repo's matching concept because OTMS turns evaluation into coordinated assignment rather than isolated pair picking. That is the same deeper problem seen in retrieval and recommendation: a system has a large set of possible pairings, and the locally tempting match may not make the whole arrangement trustworthy. It also connects to similarity because both proposed metrics depend on deciding when a text and a motion, or two collections of motions, are close in the sense that matters for human judgment. The multimodal family is relevant because the evidence arrives in unlike forms: words describe intent, while motion carries body movement over time. The bridge between those forms must be judged before any score can be trusted. Compared with papers that build better generators, this one targets the ruler used to compare generators. Its theme, motion generation metrics, sits at the quality-control layer of generative and multimodal work.
160.ww: The approach should work better than the naive metrics because it aims at the two places where the old numbers lose information. OTMS helps when local retrieval checks are too narrow. If each prompt only looks at a small set of nearest candidates, a model can appear good while the full collection still contains systematic swaps or crowding, where many motions fit the same kind of text and other text types are poorly served. A global matching score makes those arrangement failures visible because every prompt and motion participates in the same comparison. MMMD helps when the real motion collection is not shaped like one smooth cloud. Human movement categories can be separated, overlapping, or uneven. Comparing many local neighborhoods is more flexible than forcing the whole set into a Gaussian summary. The enhanced MoCLIP encoder matters because the comparison must happen in a description space where text meaning and motion behavior can meet. The abstract's strongest support is that experiments and analysis show closer alignment with human perceptual judgments.
160.po: The payoff is a better feedback signal for text-driven motion generation. If the proposed metrics track human perception more closely, then researchers can use them to tell whether a generator is producing motions that fit prompts in a way people actually recognize. OTMS buys a global view of text-motion matching, while MMMD buys a distribution comparison that does not depend on the restrictive Gaussian assumption criticized in FID. The abstract also claims the metrics are efficient, comprehensive, and reliable, so the practical gain is a more trustworthy way to compare models and guide development without overemphasizing improvements on weak legacy numbers.
160.limits: The abstract does not provide the exact OTMS cost function, the MoCLIP training details, the Gaussian-RBF scale choice, or the human-judgment study design. Those details matter because the metrics are only as good as the text-motion similarity scores and the learned descriptions they use. OTMS assumes a global matching formulation reflects perceptual quality; some prompts may allow many valid motions, which can make one-to-one matching too strict. MMMD avoids the Gaussian assumption but still depends on MoCLIP preserving the motion details people care about. The claims also assume the tested generators, datasets, and human raters represent the broader text-to-motion setting.

161.bp: This paper is about search when the user cannot express the whole need in one clean sentence. A person may begin with a broad question, react to the first answer, narrow the topic, correct an assumption, or ask for a comparison. In that setting, the system is not only matching words to documents. It is trying to keep track of an evolving purpose across several turns, decide what information is still missing, and return useful material through dialogue. The abstract frames the work as a tutorial, so its contribution is to organize the field rather than report one new algorithm. The practical system behind it is a search assistant that can understand instructions, produce text, reason through a task, and increasingly act like an agent: something that can plan retrieval steps instead of running a fixed search once. The need is clear from neighboring repo records: web assistants need freshness control, chat search needs evaluation, and search agents need to know when to keep looking.
161.wh: The hard part is that a conversation changes the search problem while it is happening. In ordinary search, the query is treated as the main evidence. In conversational search, the latest sentence may depend on earlier turns, omitted entities, corrections, and unstated goals. A user saying "what about newer ones" or "compare that with the other approach" gives little meaning unless the system remembers what "ones," "that," and "other" refer to. The system also has to decide whether to answer, ask a clarifying question, retrieve more documents, or reformulate the search. Language models add power because they can follow instructions and generate explanations, but they also add risk: a fluent answer can hide weak retrieval, stale sources, or a mistaken reading of context. Agentic behavior makes the challenge sharper. Planning dynamic retrieval can help with complex needs, but every extra search step costs time and can drift away from the user's intent.
161.naive: A smart beginner would concatenate the whole chat into one long query, send it to a search engine, and ask a language model to write an answer from the top results. That can work for simple follow-ups, but it breaks when old context becomes noise. Earlier turns may contain abandoned ideas, wrong assumptions, or side questions that should not guide the current answer. The model may treat every sentence as equally important, while the user actually changed direction. Another naive version is to retrieve after every turn with the same recipe. That wastes searches on easy turns and still fails on hard turns that need planning, clarification, or several retrieval angles.
161.ap: The core idea is to view conversational search as an interaction loop, not a one-shot lookup. The system must maintain a working picture of the user's intent, update that picture after each turn, and use it to decide the next search action. Large language models matter here because they can read instructions, connect a new utterance to previous context, generate a response, and reason about missing information in ordinary language. The newer agentic direction adds a control layer: the system can plan a strategy, choose when and how to retrieve, inspect what came back, and decide whether another step is needed. Since this is a tutorial, the paper's central move is pedagogical: it connects older fundamentals of conversational search with these newer agent-like systems, giving students, researchers, and practitioners a map of what must be designed and evaluated.
161.mech: The mechanism begins with a stream of turns: the user asks, the system answers or asks back, and each exchange changes the available context. First, the system interprets the current turn against the conversation history, separating active intent from stale or irrelevant material. Second, it forms a search need that may be more explicit than the user's words, such as expanding a pronoun, identifying the topic being compared, or recognizing that the user is asking for a broader explanation rather than a fact. Third, a retrieval component searches for information. In a modern assistant this may not be a single fixed call: the agent may choose a query, inspect results, reformulate, search again, or ask for clarification. Fourth, the system judges which retrieved pieces are relevant to the active intent and which pieces should be ignored because they are off-topic, old, outside the user's scope, or not enough to answer. Fifth, a language model uses the selected evidence and the dialogue state to generate the next response in a flexible conversational form. The output is not just a ranked list of pages; it can be an answer, a question, a plan, a comparison, or a next action. The abstract does not specify one architecture, so these steps are the field structure the tutorial promises to connect.
161.math: Several mathematical ideas sit underneath this tutorial topic. The first is ranking: the system has many possible documents, passages, queries, or next actions, and it must put the useful few ahead of the rest. A score is only a sorting handle; it says which candidate should receive attention first under the user's current need. The second is similarity, meaning learned closeness between the user's need and possible evidence. Closeness must be about the right thing: a page can share words with the query while failing to answer the current turn. The third is probability, or changing belief when evidence is partial. The system is uncertain about the user's intent, the usefulness of a result, and whether enough evidence has been gathered, so it needs estimates rather than rigid yes-or-no rules. The fourth is planning, which can be understood as choosing a sequence of actions under cost: search now, rewrite the query, ask a question, or answer. The tradeoff is completeness versus time and drift. More steps can gather better evidence, but they can also introduce irrelevant material and delay the user.
161.dots: This paper sits at the crossing of several conference threads already visible in the repo. It connects to Information Retrieval and Search because it is still about choosing useful evidence from a large collection. It connects to LLMs and Language Models because instruction following, generation, and reasoning are what make the dialogue interface plausible. It connects to LLM Agents and Tool Use because the abstract describes autonomous planning, dynamic retrieval, and agentic behavior. Nearby records sharpen the picture: OwlerLite focuses on trusted scopes and freshness for web assistants; another repo entry describes evaluation of back-and-forth search assistants by scoring conversation pieces; another asks when search agents should stop rather than keep searching; another analyzes millions of multi-step research requests to understand how agents actually search. Together, these are different faces of the same pressure: search is becoming an ongoing decision process rather than a single ranked page.
161.ww: The approach works when the system's internal state stays closer to the user's real need than a raw query would. Conversation contains helpful information that a one-shot search throws away: what the user already knows, which answer failed, what constraint was added, and what level of detail is wanted. A language model can turn that scattered context into a cleaner search instruction and a more natural answer. Agentic planning can improve the process further because different turns need different amounts of work. A simple fact may need one retrieval. A broad comparison may need several searches and a synthesis step. An ambiguous request may need a clarifying question before retrieval. This flexibility is the main advantage over a fixed retrieve-then-answer pipeline. It lets the system spend effort where uncertainty remains and avoid unnecessary work where the answer is already supported. The benefit depends on disciplined grounding: the agent's plan must be tied to retrieved information and the active conversation, not to fluent guessing.
161.po: The payoff is a clearer map for building the next generation of conversational search systems. The tutorial promises to connect fundamentals with recent agentic developments, so participants can understand both the older problem of multi-turn intent and the newer problem of autonomous retrieval planning. In practical terms, this supports search assistants that can handle complex information needs through dialogue, adapt retrieval strategy as the conversation unfolds, and return information in a flexible form rather than forcing users to repeatedly rewrite queries. The paper buys understanding and design guidance, not a single reported performance gain.
161.limits: Because the abstract describes a tutorial, it does not prove that one specific conversational search system works better than another. It gives no dataset, metric, user study, architecture, or measured result. The claims therefore depend on the broader field being accurately synthesized. For real systems, several assumptions must hold: the conversation history must contain recoverable intent, retrieval sources must be relevant and current enough, the language model must not replace missing evidence with plausible text, and agentic planning must stop before it wastes time or drifts. The tutorial can teach the design space, but deployment still requires evaluation of answer quality, source trust, latency, and user satisfaction.

162.bp: The ordinary-world problem is a workplace trying to understand what its people are actually doing with AI assistants. The evidence is not a clean survey form. It is many back-and-forth conversations: a worker asks for help, clarifies, corrects the assistant, changes direction, and eventually reaches some work product or abandons the attempt. Leaders, product designers, and researchers may want to know which kinds of work these assistants support, where they seem useful, and what designs should improve next. Reading conversations one by one does not scale, but treating them as raw text piles misses the shape of the work. This paper serves that gap. HILTON is built to turn multi-turn assistant conversations into a topic map: first shorter descriptions of what each conversation was about, then groups of similar conversations, then higher-level topic structure, with humans correcting the map so it remains practically meaningful rather than merely machine-made.
162.wh: The hard part is that a conversation is not a single clean document. It contains several turns, repeated wording, failed attempts, side questions, and context that may only become clear after the last message. If a system groups conversations by surface words alone, two sessions about the same workplace task may look different because one user says "draft this note" and another says "make this sound professional." The reverse can also happen: two conversations may share words but serve different purposes. A fully manual taxonomy has the opposite problem. Humans can judge whether a topic makes sense, but they cannot cheaply read and organize every new conversation as usage grows. The abstract also emphasizes new data arriving over time, so the topic map cannot be frozen. It must discover new patterns, keep old useful categories, and remain understandable to people who will use the analysis for design or assessment.
162.naive: A smart beginner might export all conversations, count common words, and make a chart of frequent terms. A slightly stronger version would run an automatic grouping method directly on the raw conversation text and name each group by its most common words. This fails because frequent words are often not the same as work intent. Long conversations include greetings, corrections, copied documents, assistant phrasing, and repeated instructions. Those details can drown out the real task. Another beginner might ask human annotators to label every conversation, but that becomes slow and expensive as new assistant logs arrive. The paper's starting point is therefore a tradeoff: automatic discovery is scalable but noisy, while human judgment is meaningful but scarce.
162.ap: The paper's central move is to separate the job into stages that match the strengths of machines and people. First, a large language model is used as a summarizer: it compresses a multi-turn conversation into a shorter statement of what happened. This gives the later grouping step cleaner material than the raw transcript. Second, the summaries are grouped without requiring a fixed list of topics in advance. The abstract calls this unsupervised, non-parametric clustering; in plain terms, the system looks for natural piles in the data and is not forced to decide beforehand that there must be exactly ten or twenty topics. Third, those groups are organized into a hierarchy, so narrow topics can sit under broader ones. Finally, human annotators edit and judge the discovered groups. Their feedback refines the topic structure and creates evaluation data for later rounds.
162.mech: The mechanism begins with a stream or collection of workplace conversations between users and AI assistants. Each conversation has several turns, so the first transformation is summarization. A language model reads the full exchange and produces a compact description of the conversation's main purpose. That summary is still text, but it is less cluttered than the original interaction. Next, the system compares summaries and places similar ones into clusters, meaning groups whose members appear to describe related work. Because the clustering is described as non-parametric, the pipeline is meant to allow the number and shape of topics to emerge from the data rather than from a fixed hand-written list. The discovered clusters are then arranged hierarchically: small, specific topic groups can be collected under broader categories, giving analysts both close detail and a higher-level overview. As new conversations arrive, the structure can be dynamically updated instead of rebuilt as a one-time report. Human annotators then inspect the machine-discovered clusters, adjust topic labels or boundaries, and provide feedback. That corrected output becomes a cleaner topic map and also becomes evaluation data. The final stage trains a lightweight statistical classifier, a cheaper prediction model, so unseen conversations can be assigned to topics efficiently without rerunning the whole human-review process every time.
162.math: The mathematics is about compression, similarity, grouping, hierarchy, and learning from corrected examples. Summarization is compression with judgment: many turns are squeezed into fewer words, and the system must keep the purpose of the exchange while dropping repetition and noise. Clustering is grouping by measured resemblance. The system needs some way to decide that two summaries are close enough in meaning to belong together, even if they do not use identical wording. Non-parametric clustering means the method is not locked to a preselected number of groups; this fits workplace assistant use because organizations may not know the task categories before looking. Hierarchy adds a tree-like structure: a broad topic can contain smaller subtopics, so the same data can be read at different levels of detail. Human feedback turns the problem into supervised learning for later use. Once annotators correct clusters and labels, the lightweight classifier learns a rule from examples: when a new conversation summary has certain signs, assign it to a likely topic. The key tradeoff is discovery versus control. Open-ended grouping finds unexpected uses, while human correction prevents mathematically tidy but practically useless topics from becoming the final map.
162.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of topic modeling, language-model applications, and human-centered data mining. Like other text mining papers, it tries to turn messy language into organized evidence. Like clustering work, it asks how to sort a large pile when there is no trusted label for every item. Like efficiency papers, it separates an expensive high-quality process from a cheaper deployment step: deep summarization, clustering, and human correction create the topic structure, while the lightweight classifier makes everyday inference fast. It also connects to the broader conference interest in AI assistants and agents, but from the measurement side rather than the assistant-behavior side. The sibling idea is evaluation and analytics for LLM use: before improving an assistant, defending it, or personalizing it, a workplace must first know what tasks people are bringing to it and which topic boundaries make sense to humans.
162.ww: The method should work better than raw clustering because it changes the object being grouped. A raw transcript contains the user's task, the assistant's responses, repairs, boilerplate, and sometimes pasted material. A summary aims to keep the task-level meaning while removing details that would mislead a grouping method. That gives similarity measurement a cleaner target: conversations are compared by what they were trying to accomplish, not merely by repeated words. The human loop helps for a different reason. Topic quality is partly a social and organizational judgment. A cluster can be statistically coherent and still be useless if it joins tasks that workplace analysts need to separate, or splits tasks that they view as one category. Annotator feedback supplies that missing judgment and turns it into data for future refinement. The lightweight classifier works because, after the expensive discovery and correction stages have created examples, many future conversations can be handled as a faster recognition problem rather than a full discovery problem.
162.po: The payoff is a practical pipeline for workplace analytics of AI assistant use. The abstract claims HILTON produces coherent topic structures for multi-turn assistant conversations, supports hierarchical organization, updates as new data arrives, and includes human feedback to improve quality and practical relevance. It also produces evaluation data for future iterations and trains a lightweight statistical classifier for efficient topic inference on unseen conversations. That buys two capabilities at once: open-ended discovery of what people use assistants for, and cheaper repeated categorization once the topic map has been refined. The open-source code further makes the approach reusable beyond the authors' own application.
162.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The summaries must preserve the real work intent of the conversations; if the summarizer drops a key turn or overstates what happened, every later stage inherits that error. The clustering must find groups that correspond to meaningful workplace tasks, not just patterns in phrasing. Human annotators must understand the domain well enough to correct clusters consistently, and their feedback may reflect local business priorities rather than universal topic boundaries. Dynamic updates can also disturb old categories if new data changes the structure. The abstract reports coherent topic structures, but it does not give the exact datasets, annotation rules, classifier accuracy, privacy handling, or evidence that the topics remain stable across different organizations.

163.bp: A ransomware detector watches what programs do on a Windows machine and tries to catch behavior that looks like files being locked for extortion. The practical need is not only to catch attacks, but to run the detector inside organizations that must obey deletion requests and data governance rules. If one user's telemetry, or one collected training case, must be removed, the security team cannot wait for a full rebuild of every model whenever that request arrives. This paper treats deletion as a first-class security requirement. The detector is based on reinforcement learning, meaning it learns a policy by receiving rewards for useful detection choices and costs for mistakes. The privacy problem is then sharper: how can the system remove the influence of a small set of training samples while keeping the learned ransomware behavior detector useful? The proposed answer is to train the detector in separable pieces so a deletion request touches only the piece that learned from the deleted data.
163.wh: The hard part is that a trained model does not keep a neat folder for each training example. A sample's influence is mixed into learned numbers along with many other samples, so removing one case is not like deleting one row from a spreadsheet. For ransomware detection, the model also has to preserve rare but important warning patterns. If deletion damages the detector, the privacy fix creates a security weakness. If the team ignores deletion cost, privacy compliance becomes operationally unrealistic. Reinforcement-learning detectors add another tension because they are trained around rewards and action values rather than simple class labels. The paper studies value-based agents, including DQN and DDQN, where a Q-score reflects how valuable a detection decision appears. The system therefore needs forgetting that is cheap, measurable, and compatible with confidence scores, while still retaining the ability to separate malicious Windows 11 behavior from benign behavior.
163.naive: A smart beginner would train one strong ransomware detector on all available telemetry, then, when a deletion request arrives, remove the requested samples and retrain the entire detector from the remaining data. That is conceptually clean: the new model never sees the deleted cases. It fails as a routine workflow because full retraining is expensive and slow, especially if deletion requests arrive repeatedly. Another beginner shortcut would be to delete the records from storage and leave the model untouched, but that does not remove the influence already absorbed during training. A third shortcut would be to adjust only the final decision threshold, but that changes visible predictions without proving that the deleted examples stopped shaping the learned action values. The paper instead asks for a training design where later removal is built into the structure from the start.
163.ap: The core idea is SISA: sharded, isolated, sliced, and aggregated training. In plain terms, the training data is split into separate shards, each shard trains its own model path, and the final detector combines the shard-level decisions. Isolation is the important move. If a sample belongs to one shard, its direct training influence is contained inside that shard's model rather than spread through one shared detector trained on everything. When the sample must be forgotten, the system retrains only the affected shard after removing the sample. The other shards can stay fixed because they never trained on that case. The paper applies this idea to reinforcement-learning ransomware detection and evaluates a fast-unlearning path: delete 5 percent of the samples from a single shard and retrain that shard. It then aggregates shard decisions by majority vote and checks whether detection quality is preserved.
163.mech: The mechanism starts with Windows 11 behavioral ransomware telemetry, the records of actions that programs take while running. The dataset is divided into five shards. Each shard is treated as an isolated training block, so a value-based reinforcement-learning agent learns from only that block's examples. The agents include DQN and DDQN, two ways to learn Q-values, where a Q-value is a learned estimate of how good a possible decision looks under the reward design. The reward is cost-sensitive, so the training signal can treat mistakes with different practical costs rather than pretending every error hurts equally. To evaluate fairly, the study uses 5-fold stratified cross-validation, which repeatedly splits data while preserving class balance as much as possible. At prediction time, each shard-trained detector gives a view, and the system aggregates those views by majority vote. For confidence, the paper does not stop at malicious versus benign. It uses a continuous Q-score margin, meaning the gap between competing action values becomes a strength-of-belief signal. That margin supports ROC-AUC analysis, which checks ranking quality across possible thresholds. For unlearning, 5 percent of samples are removed from one shard, only that shard is retrained, and the combined detector is compared against the costlier full-retraining route.
163.math: Several mathematical ideas are doing concrete work here. First is partitioning: split one training collection into smaller parts so influence is localized. The tradeoff is speed versus shared evidence. Smaller isolated shards are cheaper to repair after deletion, but each shard sees less data. Second is aggregation by majority vote. A vote turns several partial judgments into one final judgment; it works when the separate shard models make errors that do not always line up. Third is reinforcement learning, which here means learning from rewards rather than only from answer labels. The agent estimates action values: numbers that say how useful a detection choice appears after considering the reward and cost pattern. DQN and DDQN are value-based forms of this idea. Fourth is cost-sensitive scoring: the reward design says that different errors carry different harm, which fits security because missing ransomware and raising a false alarm are not the same kind of mistake. Fifth is cross-validation, a repeated train-and-test rotation used to reduce dependence on one lucky split. Finally, ROC-AUC from Q-score margins asks whether malicious cases tend to receive stronger warning scores than benign ones across thresholds, not merely whether one fixed cutoff worked.
163.dots: This paper sits where three conference threads meet. It belongs to machine unlearning because the central question is whether a trained system can remove specific data influence without starting over. It belongs to privacy and security because the deleted item is not an abstract example; it is behavioral telemetry collected in a defensive setting, governed by compliance and responsible deployment pressures. It also belongs to reinforcement learning because the detector is built around learned action values and rewards, not only ordinary supervised labels. Nearby unlearning papers ask similar questions in language models, graphs, recommendation, and multimodal systems: did the system truly forget, or did it only hide the evidence at the output? This paper's distinctive angle is operational compartmentalization. Instead of estimating a delicate influence correction across one model, it makes forgetting cheaper by changing the training layout. That connects it to broader efficiency work as well: saving retraining time becomes part of making privacy practical.
163.ww: The approach should work when the main obstacle is recomputation cost rather than a need for one perfectly unified learner. If each shard is trained in isolation, a deleted sample can only have directly shaped the shard that contained it. Retraining that shard from the cleaned shard data creates a new local model with the sample removed, while the unaffected shard models retain their prior work. Majority voting then lets the detector recover a system-level decision from several local views. This can preserve detection performance because ransomware behavior should leave patterns that are repeated enough for multiple shards to learn them, not patterns that exist only in the deleted cases. The Q-score margin helps evaluation because a detector can be technically right but uncertain, or wrong by a narrow amount. Looking at margins and ROC-AUC checks whether the system still orders suspicious behavior ahead of benign behavior after unlearning. The cost-sensitive reward also matters: it trains the agent toward the practical security tradeoff rather than a generic count of correct labels.
163.po: The payoff is a ransomware detection setup that treats privacy deletion as something the system can do repeatedly, not as an emergency rebuild. By retraining only the affected shard after deleting 5 percent of samples from one shard, the framework aims to reduce unlearning cost while preserving detection performance. The paper also gives a more informative evaluation surface: DQN and DDQN are compared under identical settings, detection confidence is measured with Q-score margins, and ROC-AUC examines behavior beyond one binary cutoff. For a deployed security team, the capability is concrete: respond to data deletion demands while keeping a behavior-based ransomware detector in service.
163.limits: The abstract supports an evaluation framework, not a universal guarantee of perfect forgetting. The input text is truncated, so exact numerical results beyond reduced retraining cost and preserved detection performance are not available here. The method assumes the sharding really isolates training influence enough that retraining one shard removes the relevant sample effect. It also assumes five shards and majority voting are a good balance for this telemetry setting; different data sizes, attack mixes, or deletion patterns could change that balance. Deleting 5 percent from a single shard is a controlled case, not every possible deletion request. The evidence is tied to Windows 11 behavioral ransomware telemetry, value-based agents, and the stated reward design.

164.bp: The ordinary problem is drug safety under incomplete observation. A drug can be drawn as a graph: atoms are pieces, bonds are links, and local chemical neighborhoods become small substructures inside the whole molecule. Some drugs are known to cause a side effect because that harm has been observed and reported. The rest are not proven safe; they are merely unlabeled, which means the side effect may be absent, undiscovered, or unreported. A useful classifier must therefore look through a pile of molecule graphs and flag which unlabeled ones most resemble the known risky cases. This is not only a labeling exercise. It is a way to decide where scientific attention, testing, or caution should go when confirmed negative evidence is missing. Delta-PU serves that setting by treating the graph and the training set as uneven sources of evidence: some molecular substructures are more informative than others, and some unlabeled graphs are too ambiguous to trust strongly during learning.
164.wh: The hard part is that the model is asked to learn a boundary while one side of the boundary is not named. In ordinary classification, positive examples show one kind of object and negative examples show what should be separated from it. Here, the training data has known positives and a mixed unlabeled group. Some unlabeled drugs may be true negatives, while others may be hidden positives whose side effects have not yet appeared in reports. The graph structure adds another difficulty. Positive and negative graphs can share similar substructures, so a small chemical pattern may appear in both risky and harmless molecules. If the model treats every repeated substructure as decisive, it may learn common chemistry rather than side-effect-relevant chemistry. If it treats every unlabeled graph as negative, it may punish the very patterns that identify undiscovered positives. The central tension is selective trust: deciding which parts of a graph and which unlabeled examples should shape the separating rule.
164.naive: A smart beginner might train a graph classifier by calling every unlabeled drug negative. That gives the model two boxes: observed side-effect drugs versus all remaining drugs. It fails because unlabeled does not mean safe. Some hidden positive graphs would be used as negative evidence, so the model would be trained to reject patterns it should recognize. Another beginner might avoid that mistake by using only the positive graphs, but then the model has little idea what makes a positive graph distinct from the broader population. A third simple route is to average all graph neighborhoods into one molecular summary and let the classifier decide from that summary. That also fails when the decisive signal is a subtle substructure drowned out by many ordinary shared substructures.
164.ap: Delta-PU's central move is to learn two kinds of unequal influence. First, inside each graph, it performs hop-level reweighting. A hop is a neighborhood distance in the graph: nearby atoms and bonds around a point form local patterns, and farther hops describe wider molecular context. During pooling, where many local pieces are combined into one graph-level description, Delta-PU gives more influence to hops that look informative for separating positives from the rest. Second, across the training examples, it performs graph-level reweighting. An unlabeled graph that looks ambiguous is suppressed so it cannot pull the decision rule in a misleading direction as strongly as a clearer case. The method therefore does not simply ask, 'What does this whole molecule look like?' It asks, 'Which substructures deserve attention, and which unlabeled molecules deserve caution while the classifier is learning?'
164.mech: The mechanism begins with a training collection of graph objects. Each graph represents one instance, such as a drug molecule, and each graph is marked either positive or unlabeled. A graph model reads the structure by collecting information from neighborhoods at different hop distances. Short hops capture small local substructures; larger hops capture broader arrangements around them. These neighborhood signals must be pooled, meaning compressed into a representation of the whole graph. Delta-PU inserts hop-level weights into this pooling step, so the combined graph description is not a flat average of every neighborhood scale. Hops that carry clearer separation signal are allowed to speak more loudly; less informative shared patterns have less pull. The model then faces the training-set-level uncertainty: the unlabeled pool is a mixture, not a clean negative class. Delta-PU assigns graph-level weights so ambiguous unlabeled graphs contribute less to the learning signal. As training progresses, the classifier updates its notion of which substructures distinguish observed positives and which unlabeled graphs should be trusted weakly. The output is a graph classifier for positive-unlabeled graph classification: given a new or unlabeled graph, it produces a decision or score about whether the graph belongs with the positive class, while having learned from both structural focus and example-level caution.
164.math: The mathematical ideas are weighted combining, graph neighborhood reasoning, and learning from partly hidden labels. A graph is a set of objects connected by links; in the drug example, the links let evidence travel from local chemical neighborhoods into a whole-molecule judgment. Pooling is compression: many neighborhood descriptions are turned into one graph description. The danger of compression is that it can erase the rare but important difference, so hop-level weighting changes compression into selective compression. Each hop receives a degree of influence, which is a number saying how much that neighborhood scale should affect the final graph description. Graph-level weighting applies the same principle to training examples. Because the unlabeled set is a mixture of true negatives and possible hidden positives, each unlabeled graph should not be equally trusted as evidence against the positive class. The learning problem is therefore not just finding a separating rule; it is finding the rule while controlling which pieces of evidence are allowed to pull on it. The tradeoff is focus versus blindness. Strong weights can reduce noise from shared substructures and ambiguous unlabeled examples, but they can also underplay weak clues if the weighting rule learns the wrong signs of importance.
164.dots: This paper sits in the graph classification theme because the object being judged is the whole graph, not only one node or one edge. It also belongs to a broader conference thread about selective influence under limited trust. The repo's concept data groups Dual-level Reweighting with papers where not all information deserves the same vote: graph substructures, neighbors, examples, time steps, client updates, or media fragments may help or mislead. Here that idea appears twice, within a graph and across graphs. It also connects to learning from examples under scarce labels. The known positives are useful demonstrations, but the missing negative labels mean the model must reuse examples carefully rather than treating the unlabeled pile as ground truth. Nearby graph work on long-tailed classification, open-set graph classification, and graph data with unlabeled wild cases shares the same deeper pressure: the available labels do not fully describe the deployment world, so uncertainty has to be handled inside the learning procedure.
164.ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because it attacks both places where false evidence enters. At the substructure level, positive and negative graphs may contain many of the same ordinary patterns. If all hops are pooled evenly, those common patterns can dilute the small structural differences that matter. Hop-level reweighting lets the model build a graph description from the parts and neighborhood scales that repeatedly help distinguish known positives from the rest. At the example level, the unlabeled set is dangerous because it contains uncertainty disguised as absence. Graph-level reweighting reduces the authority of unlabeled graphs that look ambiguous, so a possible hidden positive is less likely to train the model in the wrong direction. These two controls reinforce each other. Better substructure focus can make graph ambiguity easier to judge, and weaker influence from ambiguous graphs can make the substructure signal less contaminated. The abstract's phrase 'progressively focus' is important: the model's useful evidence is refined during learning rather than fixed by a hand-written chemical rule.
164.po: The payoff is a classifier for graph data when only positives and unlabeled examples are available. In the drug side-effect example, that means making better use of observed adverse-effect reports without pretending that unreported drugs are safe. Delta-PU buys a practical capability: it can search for subtle structural signs of risk while limiting the damage caused by ambiguous unlabeled molecules. The abstract reports extensive experiments and state-of-the-art performance in positive-unlabeled graph classification. Grounded in the text, the result is not merely a higher score; it is evidence that dual reweighting helps the model separate informative graph patterns from uncertainty when explicit negative labels are absent.
164.limits: The method depends on the assumption that positives contain repeatable structural signs and that hop-level weighting can identify them from the available data. It also assumes ambiguous unlabeled graphs can be recognized well enough to suppress their influence without throwing away many useful true negatives. The abstract does not specify the exact weighting formulas, datasets, or failure cases, so the strength of the evidence cannot be judged here beyond the stated experimental claim. It does not prove that every unlabeled drug treated weakly is genuinely ambiguous, or that the same learned substructures will transfer to a new chemical domain, reporting system, or side-effect category with different hidden positives.
